blocks.x: My name is Bob Schaffler. They called me Bob Schaffler. My name is Robert L. Schaffler, Robert Lee Schaffler. What the musician called me, Bob Schaffler. Where were you born? Just when? I was born in Bessie, Tennessee, April the 30th, 1900s. So just about 59 years old now. Yes, that's right. And my people brought me to St. Louis when I was two years old of course. I knew more about St. Louis than I knew about Bessie, Tennessee.

Did none of your folks play music? Your father or mother? No one in my family played music. Any brothers or sisters that were interested? I have no brothers or sisters. Do you remember the first music you heard? What kind of music you heard in St. Louis?

Well the first music I heard was what they had a Cudded Band called the Nice Epiphance Cudded Band. And I started playing in that band as a drummer. That was back in 1906. Did you have any lessons on drums? Did you just pick it up? No, see it was at that time they called it the Nice Epiphance Cadets. It's the same at the present time you'd have the Boy Scouts. Oh yes, yes. You know, but just the kids in the neighborhood. They used to all, and this nice epiphance was an organization that took all the kids off the street so they had some place to go. And they had a man by the name of Colonel Hughes we called him. And he took us and learned us how to drill, regular formation drill, and he organized the band. First he joined us at the trumpet and bugle horn. And of course I was playing drums then. Yes. We had a leader by the name of Blue, Professor Blue, who was the trumpet player. But he had lost his lip, his lip had split straight down and he couldn't play no more. But he was interested in children. So he said he was a trainer. For some reason or another he liked me and he put me off the drums and gave me a bugle. Oh yes. But he was leading up to the trumpet.
Uh huh, sure. You see.

You learned that when you were just a boy too, very often. That's right. And I was, when I was around seven years old, that's when I got on this bugle. It was like that. And he kept me on this bugle about a year. Well, it was longer than that. Because we went to the end of the, because at that time the KP used to go away every two years, what they called an encampment. It used to take the boys to band with them. Yes. And we went to In and Out with Indiana in 1911. In 1911. And that was just before we went there was when he put the trumpet in my hand. But he had learned me, the fingering, from the bugle and everything. And he told me to start to, told me to start to play. That was 1911. When did you get your first, did you get a cornet or a trumpet first? No, I got a cornet, regular cornet, a con cornet. Yep. Con cornet. And then for that.
One of the little sharpens?
That's right. And then for that my mother bought me a one. Be sure, be sure. Be sure. Be sure. Be sure. That was 1911.
When you were a boy, do you remember any of the ragtime players around there? Like Scott Joplin?
Well, during that time, yeah, that was. That was, my time was Scott Joplin and Tom Turpin.
Oh. Do you remember Louis Chauvin by any chance?
I don't remember Louis Chauvin. He could have been around there, but I didn't remember that.
He was a fellow came here at the Pekin Theater, I can't think now, Joe Jordan.
Joe Good Jordan.
Do you know him?
I knew Joe Jordan. But I knew Joe Jordan from Chicago here.
Here?
Yeah, I knew Jordan from Chicago.
I think he came from St. Louis.
That's right. That's right. And all...
Patterson, was there a pianist by the name of Patterson?
Yeah, there's Patterson. There's another piano player over there now, you know old-time one. He lives in East St. Louis now. Oh, I can't recall this name.
Somebody told me. I was raised in Missouri too. I was down there several times.
Somebody told me about him. I can't remember. I was talking about him about a month ago. He's still over there. He lives in East St. Louis. He's doing his old-time as well with Scott Joplin.
Played ragtime.
Yeah, he's still playing. Still playing? Yeah, but he lives in East St. Louis. Yes. He does like that. Oh, I can't recall this name now.
Well, when you took up a cornet, did you play in the dance band or the brass band?

Well, no. See, I started in a brass band. Well, I happened to be... What you would say happened to be fortunate that I had a good trumpet player that learned, but he let me out a reed. So then the older men used to get my mother and let me... had me to play dances with them. And they would give my mother 50 cents a night for this to have me to come. But they would see that I was... You know, with that horn. Yeah, all right. And that's where I got my experience from, which carried me into the army. Mm-hmm. See? So you were in the First World War then? That's right. See, I enlisted in the army. I was in the first band. It wasn't particularly examination in the past. It was examination to go in the 10th Calvary. I was in the 10th Calvary.
Did you play a bugle or anything there too? No, it was right on it as a trumpet player. Right on it as a trumpet player. With the band then?

It was right on it as a trumpet player. Mm-hmm. And then I got my further music knowledge there from a trumpet player by the name of Elmer Moore, who was a soulist. When I got there, the bandmaster put me on Elmer Moore, told me he wanted me to be Elmer Moore's second. That's whenever Elmer Moore, who was a chief trumpet player, couldn't make concerts and I had to play souls. I had to play those souls. Yeah, play souls. And that's where I got the part of knowing the technical part about knowing the souls. Now, this all happened all right until I come out of the army in 1919. And this is the part that leads up to my other life.
Yeah.

And when I came out of the army in 1919, Charlie Crisp was in St. Louis. Well he had set St. Louis on fire. He was working on the boat. And he wanted a trumpet player. Well Eddie Allen, who knew me before I went in on me, after coming home, he said, why don't you go down and see Charlie Crisp? But I said, well I can't play that kind of music. I said, well I know it's just straight legit music. So he said, well you go down and see Charlie. Well I wasn't seeing Charlie. And Charlie had me play the first night on the boat. He said, you've got everything and I'm going to make you one of the world greatest jazz trumpet players.
Did they use written arrangements in his band or?
No, they, it was regular stock arrangements but you dressed them up. You know what I mean?
I mean they used music though, they didn't just play with the ear in Paris.

That's right, that's right. Yeah. Now you see, Charlie was playing on the same pole and Faith Marable with Lois Armstrong and Baby Dots, Johnny Sincere, Dave Jones, oh this other clarinet player, trumpet player. He was playing the first trumpet player. He was playing saxophone now, he lives in Milwaukee now. Oh, I don't remember. It would come across from the mind.
Yeah, was Pop Foster in the band then too, bass player? Yeah, Pop Foster and Pop Foss was playing bass.
Well they was playing on the GS.
You see?

And you were at Charlie Crest was on the St. Paul. They both docked right at the end of Olive Street to St. Louis. You see? Did they both work out from there or one go up the river usually? No, now coming up, Faith brought the GS up to St. Paul, up to St. Paul, I mean St. Paul, up to St. Louis. And then the GS was brought down from the Diodocs up in the Redempo Highway. See? And they both run out of St. Louis during the summer. Yeah. You see?
Two different excursions the same night sometime, would it be that way? That's right. I didn't know.

Two different excursions, but it was two different boats. It was like that. Then the Wishart Line tried to cut in there, Captain Wishart. Now he brought in a line up, come up from New Orleans, it was called the Wishart Line. And his boat was a flat, flat bottom boat. The rest of them was...
Remember the name of any of his boats? No, I don't remember. I don't remember the Washington...

I don't exactly, I can't recall the name of his boats, but anyhow, he got Willie Grant to work on his boat. Well, meanwhile, going back to Charlie that year after I worked at 19, when Charlie, to finish that season out, Charlie would have me to come down there every night, and then he would show me passages on his horn. Well, that's how I knew the trumpet might be in the sources like that, so it didn't take me long to catch the pencil on his horn. Then when the season was over in 1920, I came up there in Chicago. Yeah. I went there working with Everett Robbins, who was working with John L. Wycliffe. Oh yes, I've heard of that. Well, Wycliffe had Freddie Keppert playing with him. Well, since I was the best reader, they always put me on first trumpet, and put the weaker guys on playing another. And that way, I got to know to play right with the New Orleans filmers, and learned their style, because I was playing first and they were playing second.
Was Keppert much of a reader, do you remember? Yeah. He could read all right then. He could read all right. We never did know for sure.
He could read all right. He was a, well, he was a much, I would say a much faster reader than Joe Oliver.
Really? I didn't know that.
Yeah, he was a much faster reader than Joe Oliver, you see. But he had a different style altogether. His style was, well, you couldn't compare the two, because he had a different style.
I've heard him on record, but I never heard either one of them in person.

No, he was just a strong, strong trumpet player. Was he rougher than Oliver? Oh yeah. Yeah, he's way rougher. Rougher. That's right. I thought that from the record. I mean, the record taker, at that time, I mean, like a 10 piece or 12 piece band, now you didn't need anybody to ever play together. Yeah. And he played all night. He just had an awful strong, strong lip. He would just play like that.
Did he ever use the muter hand much like Oliver used? Well, he used an open hand. No, that's right. Open, open hand. Open.

Well, he used an mute, you see. Where, where Freddy used an open hand. Yeah. You see. Well, now, after I come back to Chicago, then the next summer, Charlie sent for me to come back to go to work on the boat. And then, meanwhile, boy, his name, I don't take my term, I'll forget it. Fate had heard about me. And Fate wanted me to take this trumpet player.

There had been a Joe Howard from New Orleans on that boat, but he was an older man than he, I don't think he ever went to Milwaukee. No. It wasn't Joe Howard. Sidney Desveen was another one there. Yeah, he worked on that. He worked with you, I think.
I have a picture of him and you, both together on the boat. Yeah. Well, this is why I'll take my fate away.
No, I can't think either. The name will come, I guess.
Yeah.
So, don't worry about it.

Well, Charlie wouldn't release me to go to Fate. So, I had to stay up still with Charlie on the boat. You see, during that time, but then Charlie was beginning to make his band, bring his band more of between a New Orleans style and a St. Louis style. So, you had the New Orleans St. Louis style and the St. Paul, and you had the straight Dixieland New Orleans style with a Fate Man or Boydichess. And that's the way St. Louis wanted it.

What was there much difference in what you call the St. Louis style? And... No, no, no. Anything special about the St. Louis players? I've heard Charlie Crep is a wonderful blues player. That's right, you see. He's really exceptional on the blues.

Well, he was really top-zone blues and he had a good tone. He was one of the few jazz trumpet players that had a good, what we call a concert tone, a good solid tone. I see, of course, you know, during that time, you know, during the daytime, or, uh, Dway Jackson had the band on that same boat. Dway Jackson was at that same time? That's right. See, Charlie Crep was in the band.
Who else was in Charlie Crep's band? Can you remember even just two or three of them? Well, there was...
There was a guy, an old man Cooper, but he's dead, and there was Charlie Lawson. Oh, yeah, trombone. That's right, Cooper and Charlie Lawson.
Did Marge Crep, that's Zutty's single, that's right, did she play piano?
She played piano with us, that's right, she was playing piano.
That was his sister, Charlie's sister? Charlie's sister.
Oh, this boy, he died, drummer named Red. Oh, what was this boy? He would have made a very good drummer, Red, I mean, I can't think of his name now. Oh, no.
We'll find it someplace, somebody else.

Later on, he wanted to join the show. It was Red, that's short for me, awful good drummer. Very good drummer, and I was on the Dixon Land King. From St. Louis? That's right. He was a St. Louis boy. But he played drums, and...
Did Pops Foster ever play with you? I thought somebody... That's right, Pops was there. He came over here, he did, but he came over here.
Left fate and come with Charlie, yeah. This boy, I think was named Mason.
Oh, yes, I've heard him. Mason. Yeah, sure.
Well, see, Mason first was a concert, was a concert trumpet player.
Is that right?
Yeah, then he switched over, he did, to a saxophone, but he first was a trumpet player,
Yeah, I remember the name.
Mason, and he's in St. Louis now. Yeah.

Well that's what fate wanted me to come over. Well see by me playing that way that's where I come to know all those fellas and get their style because see when they come to like playing shows or hard music, they'd all the time say well Bob you take the lead trumpet. You can read it right off. Well I can read it well but then by playing beside them that's where I come to get the whole style. And of course I liked that style and was brought up with it. Well then I came up back in Chicago in 22 after leaving Charlie, that's when Dutre was going in the Lincoln Garden because Joala was out on the coast. That's when Dutre got me to come in his band with him. And we went to work in the Lincoln Garden about six months until Joala was coming back. And when Joala came back to go to Lincoln Garden Joala was signing me up to quit Dutre to go to work with him. And that's when I went in the Lincoln Garden to work with him and when we was working together until Dave Payton, Joala was after the Plantation Cafe. Well last day Dave was a ranger, he had more. Yes I knew him too. Yeah you know more musical of the prestige than Jo, you see. Was he in the theaters that he worked at the director of the orchestra at that time? In the Grand Theaters. In the Grand Theaters. So what did he tell you? He told you, alright then I'll sign the contract for you. But when you sign the contract he signed it in Dave Payton's band with Jo Oliver appearing. Yeah. Well then Jo worked in there for about six minutes and then he's sitting and told me, he said well you go and keep my band at Lincoln Garden. That's when I got her and he got her, at least I didn't get her, he got her, Lee Collins and worked with me.
Oh yes.

So Lee worked with you too. Worked with me. Because I knew Lee. He had a practice while Jo was in, while Jo was up in the plantation. Yeah. Well then, after Jo realized what he was doing in the plantation, Jo switched and had me to leave the Lincoln Garden and go up to the plantation.
The plantation, did the Lincoln Garden burn down about that time? Can you remember somebody?

Well what I mean, the Lincoln Garden had had a fire in there while we was working there. But then they built it up right up. When it went out on the road then it built back up. Right. But later on, after the band was out of there, it really burnt down completely. But Jo then was working in there.
Plantation.
Plantation.
Can you tell a bit more about that band? There's some other New Orleans fellows in there too, I believe the clarinetists.
Well now, you see when he first started man, he sent the walls and got Albert Nicholas. Well now when he first started Lincoln Garden we had Buster Bailey and Rudy Jackson. Oh yeah.
Sax, they played bass or baritone sax? No, no, Charlie Jackson.

Now it was him and Rudy Jackson, the tenor saxophone player. Oh yeah, I never did get that straight. Rudy Jackson, the tenor saxophone player, he's here now driving taxidale. Yeah, I knew he was right. And Buster Bailey's playing there. Then Charlie Jackson, he played bass saxophone. And Joe started experimenting with the bass saxophone. You see, and he had a, oh, I see, we were playing trombone. Cause we was changing trombone so much until he got what we want.
I remember one picture they had Zoo Robertson, do you remember Zoo?

Yeah, Zoo was there at one time. He was there at one time? Yeah, yeah, that's right. He's dead now. Then they had this other boy, Eddie Atkins was in there. And, uh, well, it's hard to say because, I mean, we've changed the trombone. He changed the trombone.
Yeah, he changed the trombone.

Was Roy Palmer with you there? Yeah, Roy Palmer played it one time to a, to a thing. You see, because what he was trying to do, he was trying to get a good enough trombone player to take off, uh... Take Dutre's. Yes, sir. That's right. They take Dutre's pieces. Because real Billy's man, right? Yeah. Well then, during that time, Buster Bailey got an offer to go to New York. Yeah, but Henderson was that? That's right. And Rudy Jackson said he was going. Then Joe sent to New Orleans and got Bonnie Bigard and Albert Nicholas to come up to take the two saxophone places. Meanwhile, they knew of the piano player from Panama. Yeah. You know, Louis Russell. Yes, I knew him. So they said, well, we'll bring him on up here with us. Yeah. Well, see, then Joe was trying to strengthen the band up then, for he could get ready to go into the plantation. See, still thank you God, when he's still in the band, because they, Peyton was going to leave out of the plantation and go to Persian Palace. So he was out of 64th and go. And Joe was going to follow us in there. That's when he, that's the way he's still in this band right there. And then that's when he changed and got rid of Charlie Jackson, because Charlie Jackson got to be a little, the bass saxophone, but got to be a little bit of unbearable on things. And they got Bert Cobb. Oh yeah, Bert Cobb. Bert Cobb on bass horn. And Bert Cobb was the one that went in the plantation on Bert Cobb. And then there were, uh, uh, uh, uh, there was some of his place shows up there. And now that's, that's, that's what, uh, I mean, I never did get that straight from Joe. See, I and Joe used to talk with us, you know, we used to go, we had an exhaustive thing. I don't know why Joe changed Lee Collins and got Tommy Ladner.
But he had Tommy there, that was. Yeah.

At the plantation. Yeah, when he went in the plantation, he had Tommy. Yeah, I didn't know. Not, not Lee Collins. Lee Collins with him at Gordon Gordon. But when he went in the plantation, he had Tommy there. Lee couldn't read much, I guess, at all. Well, I never knew, no, they say, I mean, I'm pretty sure Lee.

He, was a kind of slow reader, yeah. You see. But that was, I never, I never, I never get a chance to ask him for that. Being why. Oh, I, I'm going to ask one, excuse me to interrupt, is Paul Barbaran with you at Doug's time? Paul Barbaran came with us then too. Yeah, Paul was playing the bill. Because you see, Snaggs was with us at the Lincoln Gardens. Yes.

And he was with us at the Lincoln Gardens. And he was with us at the Lincoln Gardens. And he was with us at the Lincoln Gardens. And he was with us at the Lincoln Gardens. You see, and that's it, by getting Lewis Russell and everything, he thought he'd get Paul Barbaran to send his man. But, because, well you didn't know. Because see the plantation, the first time it was a cabaret, heavy cabaret. And we didn't know whether Snaggs could make the job, be able to hold a job or not. Even though he's a good, I mean Dick's a little drummer. Yeah. Because he had to play shows, you see. So then anyhow, he thought he'd be best if he'd get Paul. But then after he got in the show, it got so hard, that we had to take and get George Smith, hired George Smith to play the shows for Paul Barbaran. Well I didn't know that. Yeah. George Smith was a straight. He was a Chicago drummer, I don't know about him.
Yeah, he was a straight drummer. Oh he's a straight, just a straight drummer, you see.

He's still around, but he's just paid. No, he's paid. He used to be president of the local. Oh sure, I know the name of the local. Well he used to play, just to play the shows for Paul. And then after, anytime the new show come in there, he'd play the show for about two or three weeks until Paul got on to it, you see. Like that, I'd go enjoy it. You see. And then there were, during that time, Zutty came up and Joe said no, he wasn't ready to take and change. Now the only reason why he changed George Feely from the plantation, now for Ori, well George Feely had lost his ear. Got any deaf? I didn't know that. No, no, no, I didn't mean deaf. But you see the trombone is a guest, a guest system. Yeah, that's right. You have to be exactly right. And George was so old, George was pretty old. Got an old band, huh? He was hitting his position untrue.
Oh yeah, I didn't know. You see. Lost his feeling and all the parts.

Yeah, that's right. You see. So that's when Joe sent and got Ori, and had Ori to take him join the band. Yeah. Meanwhile they got Bud Scott in the band. Oh yeah. And they let Junie Kappa, Junie Kappa was playing banjo.
Mm-hmm.
You see. During that time then, Dave start the writing, the show's much harder. Well then, Joe wanted me to come back down to Plenty, and I was out here at the Persian Pettis with Dave.
Well where was that? The Pershing Hotel? That's right.

The Pershing Hotel. That's where it was. Al Turner's old place, you see. Yeah. But Dave goes down to the Union, and the Union puts it in, that during that Dornell, or basically by the name of Moore, and myself couldn't quit. Dave could fight but we couldn't quit. Cause Dave was trying to keep us from going back down to the plantation with Joe. Yeah. You see, because Joe was taking his job. Yeah. Well anyhow, the way we did fix it around, Al Wynn was with Sam Wooding. Oh yes. You know. In Europe, yeah. And him and Sidvick sent the telegram over to tell me, he said, I want to take him John and Sam Wooding. Well I take the telegram and show it to Joe, cause he was living right around the corner, I was living at 4636 Prairie, I lived there right after 30 years. And then Joe was living there on 46th Street. So Joe said, no, I said, we'll just try to see if we can work something. When we did work it. Tommy led and said he would like to go. Oh, so that's when Tommy went to Europe. That's right. Yeah, I see. So we take and switch between Tommy. But we told Tommy not to say nothing about it. I went to the local insurance and got Dave and Dave agreed to let me quit. Yeah. But when I come out of there, I went, instead of going to Europe, Tommy went to Europe and I went right down the ground and then Dave realized there was nothing he could take and do about it.
Just like that you see.

Yeah. And then I spent a band we struck that was Joe Oliver, myself, Paul Baldwin, Louis Russell, Bud Scott, our, our, our, Donnell Howard, Albert Nicholas, and our, Bonnie. That's right. That's right. Then later on, Donnell went to China with, with, with, with Jack Carter and we got Billy Page in the band. I didn't know him. You see. Then there's some misunderstanding, something come up later on, the door between Nick and Bonnie and Bonnie and then when Donnell come back, then Nick decided that he would go up.
Oh yes, and he went around the whole world. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

Egypt, everything. Yeah, that's it. So that's where he comes up. What it was, something happened between him and Bonnie and you don't know what happened. So that was causing that. Then that's all that's going on now and the band is still together up until 1926. In 1926 in February, I had to leave the band because I had developed a canceroid cancer on my lip. On my lip. Now, Charlie Chris, I was still, Charlie Chris, he had told me about a Dr. Brennan on New and all, it was a very good cancerous freshness and for me to come down in there and take a look at my lip. You caught it in time then. That's right. You're lucky. Well Joe thought that I was just quitting, you know, to go down to St. Louis to organize another band. I told him, no it wasn't that Joe. It was like that. So then Joe got her a tick ready to take her to work in my place. And also, Ewe Swift, the two. One to play the show, the other they could play everything. And I was off my horn from 26 until 28. Almost two years. Yeah, two years. That's when I went to Charlie Elgin. I was in the first job I played in 20 when Charlie got at the Savoy Ballroom. They take Freddie Kipper's place. Freddie Kipper had come up there drunk.
He had been to Charlie Elgin. I didn't know that. That's right.
That's right. And that's when Emmanuel Perez, Baby Dutch, Donald Howard. Oh yeah.
Baby told me about that.

He was with them. Yeah. He was with them. Yeah. So they were up at the Savoy Ballroom. Yeah. You see. We've got a little old Charlie. And I said, well Charlie. My lip is weak. But he said, well you can make it. You've got manual. And manual. The manual was very strong. The good strong drum. Yeah. So you see. He was taking care of it. And come on and started to play. And that's what I saw. So in fact. We saved that until we came out to Savoy Ballroom. And then we came out to Savoy Ballroom. And we came out to Savoy Ballroom. And I'm with the Irish and Pete.
Manuel Perez was here then in 1928. That's right. The North's here that late.
That's right. He was playing with Charlie Elgin. He's dead now. I've been dead for.

Yeah. For 14 years. I didn't know he was here that late. Well I was going to ask how Joe was to work with. Some people tell me he was a wonderful fellow. He was easy to get along with. And full of fun. And others talked like he was hard to work with.

Well the whole time I find that Joe was just like you say. Joe was an easy fellow to get along with. And he never did let you get tense. He never let you get tense. Yeah. Because he was joking the whole night long. That's what most people tell me. He just kept you in a good mood. You never got tense. You never got tense. If he see you come on the job and he, he didn't know about psychology but he was just gifted. Yeah.
Naturally.
You never got to get. Yeah. See he was, yeah see he was, yeah he was tight to you when he started telling some joke or started joking with you and first and last you'd be relaxed and all the way.
Yeah.

He was like, yeah. The same thing like if he started out and taking, playing the number like that. Now if he seen and he played the number the first time, he was tense, he allowed him to play that one number for 30 or 40 minutes. I said one number. Just keep on going, just keep it going over. Loosen up. Loosen up. So first and last you'd loosen up, loosen up and then he would knock out.
Mm-hmm.
Then when you take the number again, everybody would be relaxed and just go over the number. And that's where we made all our numbers.
Well some people have told me in the old days that Joe would just maybe start out playing by himself.
the tune you know some of the New Orleans fellas still do that just the trumpet player starts it right out now when the other guys fall in that's when he was

making up them tunes and that's why I say you see because then all 1925 24 Joe had so much I said Joe what I'm gonna do I'm going on and I'm gonna start studying so I know how to write these numbers down that you write this even before we could take a hand of all this music downs I'm gonna leave down like that so he's all the time kid music you're going down and take a hand because that's what he would do he'd come down there and sit down and he'd start to play in people being there we'd say Paul Morgan or Snaggs at that time as the kids move drum and started going then Lil would fall in when we were the small man Lil would fall on the piano then when he was in the plantation Russell would fall in then everybody gets to get on that and that's what made up the tune that's the way Snaggit all them tunes were taking me West End did they work that out Dr. Jazz do you all ever play Dr. Jazz? that's right we played Dr. Jazz, Blue Cool Jack and those numbers and Pennell Street Blues and they was asking about them numbers Sugarfoot I guess that's right and that's the way they was working
when you had the big band at the plantation after a while did they have those things arranged then did you ever have the music up in front of you?
